lead: A market-oriented cloud treats capacity as a priced good. Providers publish prices, users state a budget and deadline, brokers bid or reserve, and a scheduler matches the job to a VM under a service level agreement (SLA). The bill is metered usage multiplied by the price at the provider’s billing granularity. This idea appears in spot markets, reserved instances and enterprise chargeback, where an engineering team must see what its cloud use actually costs.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 for cloud economics and roles; Unit 2 for SLAs and usage monitors; 4.4 for capacity and 4.5 for allocation.

blocks.text: The market-oriented cloud computing (MOCC) reference model makes price and negotiation parts of the system, not a number added after the job runs. It names six core parts: consumer, broker, provider, virtual machine (VM), service level agreement (SLA), and pricing policy. Some versions add an auctioneer or market directory that records offers and matches bids.

items: Consumer: has a job, a budget, a deadline and a quality target.
Broker: turns the job into requirements, chooses a pricing scheme, negotiates the SLA, and can compare providers.
Provider: owns capacity, sets the pricing policy, and admits the allocation.
VM: is the metered unit; a usage monitor records VM-hours, GB-months and egress.
SLA: states availability, response time, and the credit paid if the provider misses it.
Pricing policy: is the rule that turns capacity and demand into a price: fixed, time-varying, auction, or priority.

blocks.text: Optional in some versions: a market directory or auctioneer that publishes offers, receives bids, and clears the trade.

A pricing policy is the rule that turns capacity and demand into a price: fixed, time-varying, auction, or priority. The broker is the part that makes the cloud a market; without it the user simply accepts a posted rate.
A pricing scheme sets what a unit costs and when the provider may take it back. Names vary, but a common seven-way market list is below.

items: Posted price: a catalogue rate per VM-hour or GB-month; the user cannot negotiate.
On-demand: a posted price billed only while the resource runs; no commitment.
Reserved or subscription: a one- to three-year commitment for a lower rate; capacity is held for the buyer.
Spot: spare capacity sold at a dynamic price; cheap, but the provider can reclaim it with short notice.
Auction: users bid and the highest bid wins at a clearing price; suits batch work.
Bidding and bargaining: the broker negotiates price, deadline and availability together, not one list price.
Differentiated or priority: the user pays more for a higher service class, such as guaranteed latency.

blocks.text: Reserved is a commitment, spot is a gamble on spare capacity, and priority is a service class. Mixing these names is a common exam error.

sections.h3: The cost model and the bill

blocks.text: Monthly bill = Σ (compute VM-hours × price per VM-hour) + Σ (storage GB-month × price per GB-month) + Σ (egress GB × price per GB) + licence fees + support fee
blocks.where: VM-hours are running virtual machines multiplied by hours; GB-month is one gigabyte stored for one month; egress is data leaving the provider’s network; licence and support are fixed or per-user charges.

blocks.text: Billing granularity is the smallest unit the provider charges. It may be per second, per minute, per hour, or an hour with a minimum charge. A VM that is running but idle still costs money: 5 percent CPU use does not reduce a VM-hour bill. Total cost of ownership (TCO) compares the cloud bill with an owned data centre: servers, power, cooling, staff, real estate and network. Inside a company, showback reports each team’s cost without charging it; chargeback actually moves money from the team’s budget. If measured availability falls below the SLA, the contract turns the shortfall into a service credit, usually a percentage of the monthly fee.

examples.question: A team runs 2 VMs continuously for a 730-hour month, stores 200 GB and sends 50 GB out of the cloud. On-demand VMs cost ₹6 per VM-hour, reserved VMs cost ₹4 per VM-hour, spot costs ₹2.1 per VM-hour, storage is ₹2 per GB-month and egress is ₹5 per GB. Compare the on-demand and reserved monthly bills, and state the spot compute cost.
steps: Spot total, if all compute were spot, = 3,066 + 400 + 250 = ₹3,716, but spot VMs can be reclaimed.
examples.answer: On-demand costs ₹9,410; reserved costs ₹6,490, a saving of ₹2,920 or 31.03 percent; spot compute alone is ₹3,066 and all-spot total would be ₹3,716.

traps: Quoting a per-hour price as the monthly cost: multiply by hours and by VM count, then add storage and egress.
Forgetting data-transfer-out (egress) and storage; these lines often decide the bill.
Ignoring minimum billing granularity: a 20-second job billed as one hour is charged 180 times its real duration.
Treating reserved and spot as the same discount: reserved is a commitment, spot can be reclaimed.
Using list price for TCO without support, licences, idle running VMs and staff.

quiz.q: What does the broker do in the MOCC reference model?
quiz.a: It turns a job and budget into requirements, bids or reserves capacity, negotiates the SLA, and returns a priced allocation.

quiz.q: Why is a spot VM cheaper than a reserved VM?
quiz.a: Spot buys spare capacity that the provider may reclaim, so the user carries interruption risk; reserved buys a long commitment and guaranteed capacity.

quiz.q: 4 VMs run 500 hours each at ₹5 per VM-hour. What is the compute charge?
A 20-second job is billed as one whole hour. What is the charge multiple over real time?
quiz.a: 3600 ÷ 20 = 180, so the job is charged 180 times its real duration.

quiz.q: List the seven common market-model pricing categories.
quiz.a: Posted price, on-demand, reserved or subscription, spot, auction, bidding and bargaining, and differentiated or priority.
Showback reports cost to a team; chargeback deducts it from the team’s budget.

quiz.q: Give two workloads that should not use spot VMs, with one reason each.
quiz.a: A payment ledger cannot tolerate sudden reclamation in the middle of a transaction; a long stateful simulation without checkpoints loses progress when the VM is taken back.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry this topic appears as FinOps: teams tag resources, allocate shared costs, and forecast spend before the invoice arrives. Kubernetes cost allocation splits a cluster bill down to namespaces and pods, which is harder than VM billing because pods share a node. Research goes further into carbon-aware pricing, where the price also reflects the time and place of clean energy. Search next for FinOps, Kubernetes cost allocation, and carbon-aware scheduling.
